searchText: is slashing the only known way to solve nothing at stake problem? Or are there other known approaches out there? I'm pretty sure by definition it is the only solution. If people can't lose anything, then by definition nothing is at stake. Unless you mean some specific subset/type of financial penalty when you say "slashing" (rather than the more broad "financial penalty" definition)? I am referring the problem "why as a validator I should not just sign every fork of the chain". Is optimistic assumption that they sre signing a proper block and then punishing them afterwards the only solution? I *think* we can prove (in theory) that if you don't suffer a penalty for signing multiple competing branches, then by definition nothing is at stake? if we could prevent the signer from signing more than once, thats a solution. How? The payload should be known by everyone beforehand for example I don't think there is any way to make it so a signer can only sign one thing, not two? i give you message to sign, with determonistic signature, theres only one signature to the payload. Thus you can only send me one signature or refuse to sign There is no central party, so the signer can send a different signature to two different parties. you cant if the payload is the same The payloads aren't the same. You are signing on two different forks, which necessarily means they are different. well if the chain is completely deterministic Order is not deterministic. I havent thought if its possible, but I dont think theres a proof that financial penalty is the only solution to the problem with that deterministic signature you move that problem elsewhere :p A deterministic blockchain wouldn't be very interesting because it would require knowing all transactions in advance. right, hashchains are like that sha(sha(...payload)) hmm, you dont have to know them in advance If you don't, then the blockchain is no longer deterministic because transaction set can change. no, it can be for example "next pi decimal". There just has to be a deterministic rule to calculate the next element We cannot (given current human understanding of the universe) predict what transactions people will want to submit before they submit them. You would need an algorithm that is able to "know" this information in advance (at genesis), even if it takes a while to calculate (just like it takes a while to calculate the i-th digit of pi. I wouldn't use "know" there thats like saying you know the nonce that produces a pow block with valid difficulty. I don't believe there is any reasonable definition of "know" that makes this statement true: "You can know in advance what transactions people will want to submit." And if we cannot know what transactions people want to submit, we cannot know what the shape of the block will be, thus we cannot know what a person needs to sign over. We can ask for the canonical signature of "this" block, but we cannot ask for the canonical signature of the "next" block because we don't yet know what the next block is until *after* the chain has come to consensus on it. if we have a consus mechanism (:D) to decide on a block, signer can just sign it or not, but cannot sign anything else If we have a consensus mechanism to decide on a block, then we don't need to sign over anything. 🙂 Everything is done by the time there is agreement on what the official "next" block is. does this mean that if one have a PoS chain without slashing, it has to have nothing at stake problem and be unsecure? I believe so. Unless you have some other consensus mechanism, in which case you don't actually have Proof of Stake you have <whatever you use to come to consensus>. one way is to have the token lose value on market if the market notices something is wrong, and slashing comes via that? We want to target the punishment only at those who behave poorly, that way we can make the cost for them very high without giving them an obvious mechanism by which to hedge their position prior to attacking the system. If we just (for example) shutdown the whole chain when something went wrong (driving the price to zero), someone could short the coin and then trigger a shutdown and come out ahead. I think ideally, we would want slashed funds to be redistributed to those who were good actors so as to incentivize defecting and challenging. We can just burn the funds as a proxy though, and then potentially mint funds for good behavior (which is what Ethereum does). I do still think there is value in giving slashed funds to other validators though as this incentivizes people more directly try to trick people into doing bad things and then backstab them. Of course, it also incentivizes people compromise other people's validators/validator keys. I actually think this is a good thing for the overall health of the network though as it allows us to bleed out poorly secured validators without an active attack on the network. Without this incentive, an attacker is only incentivized to compromise keys if they can manage an attack, so you have the problem where everything appears to be fine right up until it isn't. You don't get any early warning signs or culling of the herd. I think there is significant value to be had in creating active incentives for people to compromise Coinbase, Kraken, etc. as it is much better that they fail ASAP (if they are going to fail) than waiting until an attacker has compromised 51% of them and *then* they show their hand. hmm, so you could have a chain that pays the validator well, and when they misbehave they lose the revenue. This is generally how companies work. They provide you a service and you are a happy customer. When they do something you dont like, you stop paying and the company goes bust this works well for things that dont require long term trust This strategy *tends* to not work well for systems that can be exit scammed. However, in theory it *could* work if you can turn a guaranteed future value into nothing. The problem is that "guaranteed future value" is complicated and it is usually easier to just slash people's today-money. Augur uses this, but it has an access to funds that do not depend on the system itself Proof of Stake is a bit different from Augur in that we actually *want* a Keynesian Beauty Contest for Proof of Stake. We really don't care which fork is most popular, we just need consensus on *one of them*. With Augur, we specifically are trying to avoid a KBC so it needs more complicated (and arguably less capital efficient) mechanisms. Semi-related question to the above about post-merge behavior: proposing an invalid EL payload is not a slashable offense, right? For arguments sake lets say one proposes an otherwise "correct" block wrt hash etc but one of the tx has an invalid signature, that would just be ignored by the network but no one would be slashed? correct invalid data can have repercussions for peer scoring etc but nothing as "binary" / "irrerversible" as slashing slashing is just about ensuring a validator cannot support conflicting forks of the chain these forks come from the block tree, which as a prereq must have (1) available blocks and (2) valid blocks
